title: Three scripts, one sentence
body: Japanese mixes hiragana (grammar and native words), katakana (loanwords and emphasis), and kanji (meaning-carrying characters) — often all in one line.

example.jp: 私はコーヒーが好きです。
example.en: I like coffee. — 私 and 好 are kanji, コーヒー is katakana, the rest is hiragana.

title: Why は is read "wa"
body: As a particle, は is pronounced "wa" and へ is pronounced "e" — leftovers from older spelling. Everywhere else they're "ha" and "he" as usual.

example.en: Today is sunny. — 今日は = "kyou wa".

title: The verb comes last
body: Japanese is subject–object–verb. You often don't know what's happening until the very end of the sentence — which is why listening to the end matters.

example.jp: 私は毎朝パンを食べます。
example.en: I eat bread every morning. (lit. I every-morning bread eat.)

title: Subjects are optional
body: If it's clear from context who's doing something, Japanese just leaves it out. Saying 私は over and over sounds unnatural.

example.en: (I) watched a movie yesterday.

title: No plurals (mostly)
body: Nouns don't change for number: 本 is "book" or "books." Context, numbers, or 〜たち (for people) fill the gap.

example.en: I bought three books.

title: Counting depends on shape
body: Japanese counts things with counters: 本 for long thin things (pens, bottles), 枚 for flat things (paper, shirts), 匹 for small animals, 冊 for books.

example.en: There are two pens.

title: いただきます
body: Said before eating — a humble "I receive this." After the meal, say ごちそうさまでした to thank whoever made or paid for it.

example.en: (Before eating) Thank you for this food!

title: Three levels of politeness
body: Casual (食べる), polite (食べます), and honorific/humble (召し上がる／いただく). Learners start with ます-form: it's safe with almost anyone.

example.en: What will you eat? (polite, safe default)

title: 〜さん isn't for yourself
body: さん is a polite suffix for other people's names — never your own. Kids get 〜ちゃん or 〜くん; teachers and doctors get 〜先生.

example.jp: 田中さん、おはようございます。
example.en: Good morning, Mr./Ms. Tanaka.

title: A language full of sound effects
body: Japanese has thousands of mimetic words — not just sounds but feelings and textures. ドキドキ (heart pounding), キラキラ (sparkling), ペコペコ (starving).

example.jp: おなかがペコペコです。
example.en: I'm starving.

title: Pitch changes meaning
body: Japanese uses pitch, not stress. はし with high-low pitch is 箸 (chopsticks); low-high is 橋 (bridge). Context usually saves you.

example.en: I eat with chopsticks.

title: Katakana English
body: Loanwords get Japanese sounds: コンビニ (convenience store), パソコン (personal computer), スマホ (smartphone). Many are clipped to 4 syllables.

example.jp: コンビニでスマホを充電しました。
example.en: I charged my phone at the convenience store.

title: English that isn't English
body: Some katakana words were made up in Japan: サラリーマン (office worker), マイペース (doing things at your own pace), ペーパードライバー (licensed but never drives).

example.jp: 彼はマイペースな人です。
example.en: He does things at his own pace.

title: Kanji have several readings
body: Most kanji have a Chinese-derived on'yomi and a native kun'yomi. 山 alone is やま (mountain), but in 富士山 it's さん.

example.en: Mt. Fuji is a tall mountain.

title: Kanji + hiragana tails
body: Verbs and adjectives write their core in kanji and the changing part in hiragana (okurigana), so conjugation is easy to see: 食べる → 食べた → 食べない.

example.en: I already ate.

title: すみません does triple duty
body: It means "excuse me" (to get attention), "sorry" (small apology), and even "thank you" when someone went out of their way for you.

example.jp: すみません、ありがとうございます。
example.en: Sorry for the trouble — thank you so much.

title: よろしくお願いします
body: No neat English equivalent: "please treat me well / I'm counting on you." Said when meeting people, starting work together, or asking favors.

example.jp: はじめまして。よろしくお願いします。
example.en: Nice to meet you. (I look forward to getting along.)

title: Listening out loud
body: Japanese listeners give constant feedback called aizuchi — はい, ええ, そうですね, なるほど — to show they're following. Silence can seem like you aren't.

example.en: I see, is that so.

title: Dates have special readings
body: The first ten days of the month use native readings: 一日 is ついたち, 二日 ふつか, 三日 みっか… 十日 とおか. Also 二十日 はつか.

example.jp: 四月一日は日曜日です。
example.en: April 1st is a Sunday.

title: Days of the week are the planets
body: 月 moon, 火 fire (Mars), 水 water (Mercury), 木 wood (Jupiter), 金 gold (Venus), 土 earth (Saturn), 日 sun — just like the old Latin names.

example.jp: 金曜日に会いましょう。
example.en: Let's meet on Friday.

title: The こそあど system
body: こ = near me, そ = near you, あ = over there, ど = which/question. It works across words: これ／それ／あれ／どれ, ここ／そこ／あそこ／どこ.

example.en: The restroom is over there.

title: No future tense
body: Japanese only marks past vs. non-past. 行きます covers both "I go" and "I will go" — time words make it clear.

example.en: I'll go to Kyoto next week.

title: Feelings as weather
body: Japanese often describes feelings as states rather than actions: 寂しい (lonely), 懐かしい (nostalgic), もったいない (what a waste!). Some don't translate cleanly.

example.jp: まだ使えるのに、もったいない！
example.en: It still works — what a waste to throw it out!

title: ただいま／おかえり
body: Coming home, you say ただいま ("I'm back"). Whoever's home answers おかえり ("welcome back"). It's a small daily ritual.

example.jp: ただいま！— おかえりなさい。
example.en: I'm home! — Welcome back.

title: The genkan
body: Homes have a genkan, a lowered entry area where you take off your shoes. Stepping up onto the floor means you've really come inside.

example.jp: ここで靴を脱いでください。
example.en: Please take your shoes off here.

title: Kanji are built from parts
body: Many kanji combine a meaning part (radical) with a sound part. 氵 relates to water: 海 sea, 池 pond, 泳 swim, 洗 wash.

example.en: I swam in the sea.

title: Casual speech drops a lot
body: Among friends, です and ます disappear, particles get dropped, and questions end in a rising tone instead of か.

example.en: Want to eat this?

title: What N5 → N1 means
body: The JLPT is Japan's standard proficiency test. N5 is the basics (~800 words, ~100 kanji); N1 is near-native (~10,000 words, ~2,000 kanji).

example.en: I'm taking the N4 next year.

title: Why words come back
body: Nagare quizzes you right before you'd forget, then waits longer each time you get it right. That spacing is what moves words into long-term memory.

example.jp: 毎日少しずつ覚えましょう。
example.en: Let's learn a little every day.
